name: Antree
tagline: Queue and appointment management: customers book or take a ticket, staff call the next one, a screen shows who is up.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The data model here is small: services, time slots, tickets, a counter that increments. An agent can produce a working booking page, a staff console, and a waiting room display in one sitting, and it will genuinely work for a single location. The gaps are all at the edges: SMS or WhatsApp notifications need a paid gateway and a verified sender, kiosk tablets and ticket printers need hardware babysitting, and multi-branch staff roles turn a toy into a real permissions problem. It also has to be up and correct while a line of actual humans is standing in a room, which is a different reliability bar than a side project usually meets. Build it for your own clinic or barbershop, not for three sites and twelve staff.
coreLoopDIY: A self-hosted queue system: public booking and walk-in ticket page, staff console to call and serve next, and a live display screen driven by server-sent events.
requirements: A machine or small VPS that stays on during business hours
A screen or spare tablet for the waiting room display
An SMS or WhatsApp provider account if you want notifications instead of a screen
whatYouLose: Outbound SMS and WhatsApp notifications, including sender verification and delivery retries
Kiosk apps, ticket printers, and display hardware that someone else supports
Multi-branch setup with staff roles, shifts, and per-counter routing
Reporting on wait times and no-shows that management will actually ask for
Someone to call when the queue freezes with people standing in front of it
moatNotes: The software is easy. Messaging deliverability and hardware that survives being poked all day are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the failure mode is public. A booking bug on a personal tool means you missed a haircut; a queue bug in a clinic means twenty annoyed people and a receptionist writing numbers on paper. Paid tools bundle the boring parts nobody wants to own: message delivery, tablets that reboot cleanly, wait time reports, and a support line during opening hours. If you run one small location and are the only staff member, the DIY build is fine and probably nicer than what you would rent.
notes: Fine as a one-location build; the moment a second branch appears you have signed up to write an admin panel.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted queue and appointment system for a single location. Stack: Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3, no ORM, no external services.

Data model in SQLite, created by a migration script on first run:
- services: id, name, avg_minutes, active
- slots: generated from business hours config, per service, per day
- appointments: id, service_id, customer_name, phone, slot_start, status (booked, arrived, serving, done, no_show)
- tickets: id, service_id, number, kind (walkin or appointment), created_at, called_at, served_at, status
- config: single row for business name, opening hours, slot length, timezone

Pages:
1. / : public booking. Pick a service, see the next 7 days of open slots, submit name and phone, get a confirmation code. Block double booking with a unique constraint on (service_id, slot_start).
2. /walkin : tap a service, issue the next ticket number for today, show a big number and the count ahead.
3. /staff : password-gated by a single STAFF_PASSWORD from .env, stored in an httpOnly cookie. Shows today's queue in order, buttons for Call Next, Serving, Done, No Show. Shows the currently called ticket per counter (counters 1 to 3, hardcoded in config).
4. /display : full screen dark page for a TV. Shows the current number per counter plus the next five waiting. Updates over Server-Sent Events from /api/events, no polling.
5. /admin : edit config, services, and business hours. Same password gate.

Rules:
- Ticket numbers reset daily per service, prefixed with a service letter, e.g. A014.
- All times stored UTC, rendered in the configured timezone.
- Seed the database with two services and sane hours so it is usable immediately.

Explicitly out of scope: SMS, WhatsApp, email, payments, multi-branch, staff accounts, analytics dashboards, telemetry.

Deliver a README with run instructions, a .env.example containing STAFF_PASSWORD, and a one-command dev start. Keep it under roughly 1200 lines of app code and prefer server actions over API routes where possible.
